title: The Clockwork Artist
markdown:
Asha the crow had a tiny gear between her tweezers — teeth like a miniature dragon’s — when Mrs. Higgins from the tea shop pressed her face to the clock-tower window.

“Oh, my goodness,” Mrs. Higgins whispered, loudly. “She isn’t just setting the time. She’s doing a celestial alignment.”

Asha sighed. A puff of brass dust escaped her beak. Celestial alignment. She was trying to stop the Grand Oakhaven Clock from striking thirteen. The Arts Weekend had turned the station into a burst of pottery and spoken-word poetry, and her one goal was simple: keep the station’s heart on time. No drama. She had told her mentor, old Mr. Fitzwilliam, that she could handle it alone. He had winked and muttered something about artistic interpretation.

A familiar rustle. Noah the stoat, cousin, energy in a crooked tweed waistcoat, arrived in a flurry.

“Asha! I heard you were creating a magnificent temporal symphony. I’ve brought snacks. For the grand finale!” Sunflower seeds and a slightly squashed jam sandwich, presented with a flourish.

“I’m adjusting the escapement,” Asha said. “It’s technical.”

“Of course. The tension before the reveal.” He nudged a stack of programmes that had been leaning with dignified tilt. “Special books, arranged with such wonderfully artistic chaos.”

She went back to the chime. The station buzzed below: banners, coffee, turpentine. She did not look down. Mr. Fitzwilliam’s wink still sat in the brass dust. Artistic interpretation, he had said, as if a clock were a canvas. Asha preferred teeth that meshed.

The next day a tiny screw had come loose. A faint stutter in the minute hand. Asha lifted it with fine tweezers. Artists at easels near the entrance watched her focus.

“Amazing,” said a woman with paint on her nose. “A powerful symbol for overcoming artistic challenges.”

“Or,” added a gentleman with a tilted hat, “a planned suspense for the opening. Temporal art.”

“It’s just a loose screw,” Asha muttered.

“Ah, just a loose screw,” Noah echoed from a bench, as if she had said something wise. “The vital start of a revolutionary clock.”

The Arts Weekend arrived bright and wonderfully clear, the kind of morning painters and performers love. Platforms wore colourful banners that danced in the breeze. Fresh coffee mixed with the sharp scent of turpentine. The Grand Oakhaven Clock stood watch, hands moving steadily toward the start of the festivities. The stationmaster, a round man with a talent for finding deep meaning in everyday things, stood by the clock face with a thick bunch of papers.

“Asha, my dear young lady! The grand temporal arrangement — is it proceeding as planned? The arts council is eager for your precisely timed synchronicity.”

The clock made a loud, jarring clunk. The minute hand jumped, then snapped back. A gasp moved through the crowd.

“The grand reveal is falling apart!” Mrs. Higgins cried, hand to chest.

“She’s doing it on purpose,” declared the tilted-hat artist. “A statement about the fleeting nature of time. Brilliant.”

The stutter was worse than before. Asha had only wanted to fix it. She looked at Noah, who had moved closer. He was not watching the crowd. He was watching the mechanism.

“Asha. That spring near the pendulum. A little too tight. It’s catching.”

So simple. Everyone else wanted a story. Noah had seen a spring. Asha reached into the open workings, sure and quick, and eased a little tension.

The clunk stopped. The minute hand went on. When the hour chime rang, it was a clear, strong, perfectly timed note.

The stationmaster blinked. “It’s… working?”

“It seems,” said Mrs. Higgins, faintly disappointed, “that she simply fixed it.”

The weekend began in full swing. Pottery caught the light. Someone recited a poem about trains that almost kept time and then, thankfully, did. The Grand Oakhaven Clock chimed the hours with steady beauty, a reliable presence through the day. Asha watched from a quiet shadowy spot, a small happy smile on her beak. Noah ambled over and nudged her elbow. He did not make a speech. He offered the jam sandwich, still slightly squashed, and they ate it while the clock, uninterpreted, kept time.
